speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to report briefly to the house that in Washington yesterday and the day before there was held the fifth meeting of the joint Canada-U.S. committee on trade and economic affairs.
The United States was represented by Hon. Christian Herter, secretary of state; Hon. Douglas Dillon, undersecretary of state; Hon. Robert B. Anderson, secretary of the treasury; Hon. Fred A. Seaton, secretary of interior; Hon. Ezra T. Benson, secretary of argiculture; Hon. Frederick H. Mueller, secretary of commerce, and Mr. Don Paarlberg of the White House. The Canadian government was represented by my colleagues the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture and myself.
The meetings covered a very broad range of questions pertaining to trade and economic matters of mutual interest to the two countries. The meetings afforded an opportunity for friendly and frank discussion and very helpful and constructive exchanges of views and information.
The representatives of both countries were able at the conclusion of these meetings to express satisfaction at the very high degree of understanding and co-operation between the two governments.
Mr. Speaker, may I table for the information of the house a copy of the communique which was issued at the close of the meetings. If it is the wish of hon. members perhaps it could be printed as an appendix to today's Hansard.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-6, to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment).
He said: Mr. Speaker, in view of the remarks of the party leaders concerning the arrangements and agreements which have been reached in the house, I feel somewhat at a disadvantage. I based my remarks and preparation therefor on the assumption that we would be discussing only this bill, the specific issue of the abolition of capital punishment. However, if time allows at the conclusion of the debate, I hope I might be permitted to make a few observations in a general sense concerning those other bills.
I think it would be appropriate, Mr. Speaker, if I indicated what my personal motivations were in introducing this bill and how we have come to this position in the house today. A few years ago I served on two successive murder juries in the city of Toronto. As I have indicated in this house previously, both accused were found guilty of murder and sentenced to hang. Both sentences were appealed successfully at a later date on the ground of misdirection of the jury.
Following that experience, having been brought face to face with the practical issue of capital punishment, I decided it would be appropriate at least to examine more

Capital Punishment
thoroughly the case for and the case against capital punishment. In the intervening years I have made it my business to read just about everything I could find on the subject, on both sides; I should like to underline that fact.
I think it would be appropriate to mention in passing, Mr. Speaker, that the remarks of Mr. Chief Justice McRuer in his instructions to one of the juries on which I sat were to the effect that the jury room is not the place in which to alter the law of Canada; that the law is as it is and must be treated as it stands. He added, almost as an afterthought, that the place in which to change the law was the parliament of Canada. Although at that time I had no anticipation or expectation of it, I now find myself in parliament and I propose to do just that.
One of the books I read was written by Sir Ernest Gowers who served as chairman of the royal commission in the United Kingdom in 1949; I refer to the royal commission established to inquire into capital punishment. The remarks he made so closely parallel my own experience and my own conclusions in this matter that I should like to read into the record of this debate the remarks that appear in the preface to that book:
Before serving on the royal commission I, like most other people, had given no great thought to this problem. If I had been asked for my opinion, I should probably have said that I was in favour of the death penalty, and disposed to regard abolitionists as people whose hearts were bigger than their heads. Four years of close study on the subject gradually dispelled that feeling. In the end I became convinced that the abolitionists were right in their conclusions-and that so far from the sentimental approach leading into their camp and the rational one into that of the supporters, it was the other way about.
Quite apart from the parallel situation in the much more modest way in which I experienced it, I attach considerable significance to that statement.
I would ask the indulgence of the house in allowing me to clear up a few matters before I come to the nub of the argument on the issue of capital punishment. On both sides of this issue I have been accused of going too far, and not far enough in the matter of not attempting to amend the law concerning treason. It has been many years since anyone was executed for treason in this country. In the main the law concerning treason relates to and presupposes a situation in which war is declared or is about to be declared. I felt it would be better to leave that matter apart from this debate, and to settle the clear issue. In this bill we are proposing to abolish capital punishment for murder and this, as I said earlier, is the clear, single issue before us.
When this bill was introduced for first reading, Mr. Speaker, it was seconded jointly

by a member of the Liberal party and a member of the C.C.F. party, as I indicated, as the rules would allow. My reason for this was that in my reading on this subject I encountered the development which unfortunately took place in our sister commonwealth country of New Zealand. In case hon. members are not aware of the fact, I may say that it did become a political issue in that country. One government commuted all death sentences for a number of years and in 1943 proposed a bill to abolish capital punishment. This bill carried over strenuous opposition, and when that government was defeated the former opposition introduced a bill to restore capital punishment.
This happened about 1949. Capital punishment was again in effect in New Zealand from 1950 to 1957, when the first government was re-elected, and since that time have commuted all death sentences. The pattern would indicate that one of these years it will reintroduce a bill to abolish capital punishment. These are consequences of this matter becoming a party issue; and I submit, Mr. Speaker, with the greatest respect to our sister country of the commonwealth that it is most undesirable to arrive at a situation where a change of government involves a fundamental change in the criminal code.
It is interesting to note in connection with New Zealand that during the immediate postwar period, from 1946 until 1950, the average number of murders per year was 6.7. This was a period when capital punishment was abolished. In the years from 1950 to 1956, the latest figures I could obtain from the New Zealand high commissioner's office show the average number of murders was 8.7. That is one indication, Mr. Speaker, of the sort of statistics which result where experiments under given circumstances have taken place.
I would like to raise another point at this time, Mr. Speaker. It concerns the number of letters I have personally received and letters which have appeared in many newspapers in my constituency and other newspapers across the country, dealing with the question of sympathy for the murderer. There are a great number of people who are under the impression that among my motives and the motives of those who support the abolition of capital punishment is sympathy for murderers at the expense of sympathy for the murderers' victims and their families. I would like to state categorically, Mr. Speaker, that of course there is not an hon. member in this house, or in any other house, who has not the most profound sympathy for these people. But my main

concern is for this society in which I live. As a member of this parliament I would like to make my contribution, and change the law as I and many other hon. members in this house feel it should be changed.
Another common misconception with regard to this bill, which is quoted in letters and newspapers, concerns the supposed restoration of the death penalty in England. It is a fact that the death penalty was never abolished in England. It passed a free vote in the House of Commons by a small margin, and during the interval between the time it passed the house and went to the Lords the home secretary very properly deemed it advisable to commute all death sentences.
I think it is of more than passing interest while discussing England to mention some statistics which emerged from that experience. During the eighteen months before the suspension period the number of murders committed were 256. The death penalty was suspended for a period of 18 months, and' the number of murders during that period was 246. During the 17 months after restoration, which was the period of time which elapsed for which these figures were made available, the number of murders committed was 310, and I would assume that if the eighteenth month had been added this figure would have been higher. That again underlines the fact that the non-existence of capital punishment at a given point in time in a given country does not relate in any provable way to the contention of those who support the retention of capital punishment.
I would now like to put on record very briefly the reasons-and they are not emotional reasons-why those of us who favour this bill are in favour of the abolition of capital punishment.
First, we contend that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent, and certainly not a unique deterrent. Second-and perhaps I speak for myself on this matter, Mr. Speaker-I feel it is morally wrong that the state should take a human life. Some religious groups argue that it is morally defensible, but I think no religious group takes the view that it is morally mandatory. The qualification is always if it is necessary that the state should take a human life, then that is a moral justification. Many other religious groups are very fundamentally opposed to capital punishment, in addition to the groups I have mentioned. The question whether or not capital punishment is necessary revolves, in my opinion, around the question of the deterrent, and I will come back to that later in my remarks.
The third reason, Mr. Speaker, is that capital punishment is based on revenge, on
Capital Punishment
retribution. Punishment, in my opinion, should be reformative, not retributive, and certainly the sanctity of human life and the Christian concept of redemption should apply as far as this question is concerned.
I read in the record of debates in other years a statement which I still believe is one of the more powerful statements on this subject, and I would like to put it on record again at this point. It is the statement of Rabbi Feinberg of Holy Blossom temple, Toronto, and is as follows:
Is any human being exempt from the desire to be appeased by a criminal's contorted agony? I remember the gratification I derived from the hanging of the nazi war criminals. They had steeped their hands in the blood of six million Jews, the evil they visited on mankind was beyond reckoning-yet I recall my feelings with shame, as unworthy, and as more excusable only in degree than the cries of the mob milling about the gallows at Cornwall prison recently.
The next reason, and perhaps the most obvious of all, Mr. Speaker, is the risk of error. Lafayette said, "I shall ask for the abolition of the death penalty until I have the infallibility of human judgment demonstrated to me". Innocent men have been hanged and innocent men will be hanged as long as human beings are human beings and subject to error.
I have reviewed at length, and I shall not repeat those arguments here, some of my personal observations and opinions concerning the capacity of the legal system as presently constituted to reach a sufficiently certain conclusion to justify absolutely the taking of a human life. I spoke of the tendencies of judges, the tendencies of juries, the position of the crown versus the defence in terms of their respective capacities and knowledge of the law. I spoke of the resources available to the police versus the resources available to the defence lawyer, particularly in the case of legal aid.
There is another reason, Mr. Speaker, which can be demonstrated, and it concerns the adverse effect on justice of capital punishment. Juries, being composed of human beings, are reluctant in many cases to bring in a verdict which will result in a hanging; and as the law stands today a verdict of guilty of murder automatically carries with it a hanging sentence. This, in terms of the protection of society which must flow through our consideration of this matter, is clearly illogical and not in my view desirable.
Another reason advanced concerns the unequal results of almost identical actions. The position of an attempted murderer whose bullet misses by a fraction of an inch a vital organ of his victim, compared with that of the murderer whose bullet goes through a victim's

Capital Punishment
heart, is an example. How, under the present law, can we judge that one person in this situation should be hanged and the other set free in a relatively short time to return to society? This difficulty accounts for the contradictions in the attempts which have been made to resolve this question of the degree of culpability in situations like this.
I should like to return to this question of the deterrent effect of capital punishment upon which, as I said earlier, the debate will largely hinge. In the early days in England- and it was not very long ago-public hangings were the order of the day, and among the categories of crime which were punishable by hanging was pickpocketing. Reports from those days indicate that when pickpockets were publicly hanged-and certainly if hangings were ever to be a deterrent, a public display of hangings was to be expected to have that effect-pickpockets were busier than ever. As a matter of fact the moment of the drop, all eyes being riveted on the victim, was exactly the moment when the pickpockets made hay in the audience. Public hangings were finally stopped when a committee investigated the matter and produced evidence, one part of which was that out of 167 candidates for hanging 164 had personally witnessed a public hanging. Clearly the deterrent aspect of public hanging was not working, and it was discontinued.
This question, and arguments concerning deterrents, were dealt with by a number of writers on the subject, and one of them has put it this way:
The gallows obviously failed as a deterrent in all cases where murder has actually been committed.
Surely this is the most obvious statement of all.
It is certainly not a deterrent to murderers who commit suicide, and one third of all murderers do. It is not a deterrent to the insane and mentally deranged or to those who commit murder in a quarrel, or in drunkenness or in a sudden surge of passion. This type of murder amounts to 80 per cent to 90 per cent of all murders that are committed.
It is not a deterrent to the type of person who commits murder because he desires to be hanged, and these cases are not infrequent. It is not a deterrent to the person who firmly believes in his own perfect method-by poison, acid bath, and so on-which, he thinks, will never be found out.
It seems to me with regard to this question of deterrence that ultimately one comes down to the fact that the only effective deterrent is the certainty of apprehension and conviction. Elsewhere in Sir Ernest Gowers' book, which I mentioned earlier, the following comments appear:
The verdict on capital punishment as an instrument of retribution must be that it satisfies a

popular demand in a way that no other punishment could. How widespread that demand is no one knows, but it is certainly not negligible. Whether it is right or necessary for the state to encourage its satisfaction is another matter.
This is the matter with which we are concerned today. It has been argued, concerning the deterrent factor, that the abolition of capital punishment would result in a spectacular increase in crime. Throughout history when the categories of crimes punishable by death have been reduced the cry has been the same, and undoubtedly it will be the same today. Up until 1956 some 36 countries had abolished capital punishment, and nowhere in the statistics or in the analysis of the crime rates in those countries and states has any evidence been produced before any royal commission on this subject, which I have encountered, to support such a proposition.
In the case of the United States, which perhaps is a convenient example, there were until 1958, when Delaware abolished capital punishment, six states which had abolished capital punishment, many of them for many years. The murder rate per 100,000 population in the other 42 states at that time was exactly 7.04; in the six states which had abolished capital punishment, including a state such as Michigan with a large metropolis comparable, perhaps, to many in our own country, it was 1.838. Surely this is an answer in advance to those who contend that the murder rate would immediately bound upward if capital punishment were abolished.
There are other examples, and I think these are even more pertinent in view of the fact that arguments have been raised concerning this matter in and out of the newspapers and certainly in my correspondence. What happens when a country or a state, adjoining another state which has retained capital punishment, abolishes the death penalty? It has been asked, is it not reasonable that those who are bent on a life of crime should gravitate to the area which has abolished capital punishment.
Again, this argument is based on what I think is a false premise, namely that capital punishment is a unique deterrent. However, let us take the example of North and South Dakota. For a number of years North Dakota abolished capital punishment and South Dakota retained it. When one examines the crime pattern which emerges one finds that the murder rate fluctuates in a very similar way on both sides of the boundary, and in more cases than not, in those two very similar areas, the rate in the abolitionist state is lower.
A similar comparison can be made between Massachusetts and Rhode Island, states side by side in another area of the country, Rhode

Island having abolished capital punishment and Massachusetts having retained it. The picture which emerges is the same. Again I underline the fact that the only effective deterrent in the way of murder or any other crime is the certainty of conviction.
I should like to mention in passing certain statistics concerning an action taken in Chattanooga, Tennessee not too many years ago which had the effect of reducing crimes of violence in a specific 12-block area, which had a high crime incidence, by between 80 per cent and 90 per cent. This action was not, as some might suppose, concerned with any more severe application of the penalties of the law. Indeed, this surprised me when I read it. The authorities simply provided additional street lamps. Action as simple as that produced the spectacular result that I have cited.
These are the basic reasons upon which the case for the abolition of capital punishment is based, and I repeat not emotional reasons. In the time that remains I should like to deal with the arguments that those who would favour retaining capital punishment may advance, and perhaps in anticipation of their arguments answer some of the objections and satisfy some of the qualifications and reservations which I know exist in hon. members' minds.
In the main the arguments advanced in favour of the retention of capital punishment boil down to three. It is claimed that capital punishment is a unique deterrent, that no satisfactory alternative exists, and that in any event public opinion is not in favour of it. I challenge hon. members who are going to participate in this debate to demonstrate by reasonable arguments the validity of the first claim, that capital punishment is unique in terms of a deterrent. My very humble submission is that this cannot be established. I feel the onus should be on those who wish to retain this thing to make their case and state it. I have looked everywhere for a reasonable case and have been unable to find it. Perhaps those in this house who take this position may find a convert in me if they can advance a reasonable case.
As far as a satisfactory alternative is concerned, as I mentioned before, some 38 countries and states have abolished capital punishment and have in operation a satisfactory alternative.
With respect to the third argument concerning public opinion, there has been a dramatic change in public opinion on this question in this country, which I am confident still is continuing. As the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) mentioned last year in referring to public opinion polls on
Capital Punishment
this matter, not too many years ago 72 per cent of the people of Canada indicated that they were in favour of retention, and a few years later that figure had dropped to 52 per cent.
In any event the arguments on this matter, I feel, should be based on the merits of the logical and unemotional reasons advanced on either side regardless of the specific position of public opinion on this question at the moment. In my view parliament and we here considering this matter should lead public opinion rather than follow it, making sure, of course, that we stay within hailing distance.
The question is raised by those who would retain capital punishment, how can the protection of the public be guaranteed if capital punishment is abolished? I submit that it can be achieved by following something along this pattern as a basic approach, altering our laws concerning these matters when the occasion arises:
No person convicted of murder be released from care in a correctional institution so long as his retention therein is essential to the well-being of society and to his reformation.
Surely we are capable of so framing our laws and establishing our institutions as to achieve that end.
There is a fascinating argument I encountered in many debates that occurred in the British House of Commons and House of Lords, and in many books. It is a heads I win, tails you lose argument. It has to do with the question of the incidence of crime. Over the years when this question has been debated it has been argued that crime has been increasing or decreasing. I am sure that at this very moment there may be an increase of crime in certain areas and a reduction of it in others. Those who support the death penalty have argued, in times when crime has been increasing, that this would be a most dangerous moment to undertake so hazardous an experiment. On the other hand, when crime has been decreasing the argument has been to the effect that the fact that crime is decreasing shows how effectively capital punishment serves as a deterrent, and therefore it would be a great mistake to hazard the experiment just when crime is reduced and everything is going so well in this field. One cannot have it both ways, and I would suggest that those who are speaking in favour of retention should take one or other of these positions and stay with it.
A further argument which is often raised in discussions on this subject, and which I feel should be answered at an early stage in this debate, is one advanced by no less a person than the former commissioner of

Capital Punishment
the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Mr. Nicholson, in an article which appeared in a local paper and was widely circulated and commented upon. It was also commented upon and supported by the chief of the Toronto metropolitan police force. Mr. Nicholson advanced the suggestion that if Canada abolished the death penalty there would be an immediate migration of murderers and of the criminal element across the border from the United States to conduct their affairs in this country. If these gangsters and criminals are interested in finding a place where capital punishment is not in effect, surely they do not have to come across the border. If it is true, as some have contended, that the center of crime is focused in Chicago, it is a much shorter trip from Chicago to Detroit and one that can be made more easily than a trip to Canada involving expense, trouble and the immigration problems these people would no doubt encounter in attempting to cross the border.
Another argument that has arisen from time to time is that of cost. There are those who say that taxpayers should not be saddled with the burden of paying taxes to support the criminal element in prison. At first blush this would appear to appeal to certain people, but when one considers that in many cases this is the last argument put forward on this question, one realizes that one is reducing to a question of dollars and cents the problem of whether we can afford to keep certain persons alive in our society. It does not take too much imagination to see where that sort of thinking leads.
There is also the question of the protection of policemen and guards. With respect to a policeman apprehending a criminal at large, surely under the law as it is now he would be in much more danger than he would be if capital punishment were abolished. With respect to guards in prisons containing these individuals if capital punishment were abolished, surely the ingenuity of man, in the light of the invention of amazing machinery and devices and rockets that land on the moon, is capable in this day and age of devising some method of confining these individuals in prison without endangering the guards who are their custodians.
I feel that my time is drawing to a close. I have endeavoured to outline some of the arguments for and against the retention of capital punishment. Far more eloquent and able speakers than I will follow and speak in favour of this resolution, and I am sure they will have a more profound impression

on the house than I. I should like to conclude by reading the final remarks of Sir Ernest Gowers in the book to which I made reference:
There remains the argument that without the uniquely deterrent value of capital punishment more murders would be committed. That is the only serious utilitarian argument in favour of capital punishment, and the one on which thoughtful supporters of it almost wholly rely. It is also the argument that can be put most readily to the test of evidence in the proper sense of the word; and, as we have seen, such evidence as there is goes to show that the abolition of capital punishment does not in fact have this result.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order that there will not be any misunderstanding may I say immediately and categorically that I am opposed to the principle of capital punishment. Apparently if one has strong feelings on this matter there is among some a violent reaction. I was interested to note in reading this morning's newspaper that the mover of this bill had received a couple of threatening letters. May I, sir, through you tell him not to worry about that; I have received five myself in the past two weeks, and the only place for those is the wastepaper basket, where a lot of newspapers should go, too. But I read them first, both of them.
I was going to say, Mr. Speaker, that this sort of reaction is rather amusing at times; and in introducing a serious subject perhaps we might do it in an amusing way. About two weeks ago I received one of those letters and read it. It amused me and I still chuckle about it every time it comes to my mind. This letter said, "I notice that Mr. McGee and yourself are still trying to abolish capital punishment. I believe in capital punishment but I want you to know I am glad that both Mr. McGee and yourself believe there should be capital punishment for treason. I am glad you take that position and I hope you are the first s.o.b. who gets hanged under that".
Well, we get those letters and I introduced that subject in a kind of humorous way to introduce a most serious matter. I want to follow perhaps the same procedure as that of the previous speaker. I first became interested in this matter about a quarter of a century ago, when I had the honour of being a member of the provincial legislature of British Columbia. I was asked 25 years ago if I would interest myself in something which had taken place in that province. Three Indians felt that two policemen were using their authority in a way they should not by demanding certain privileges from Indian women. These three Indians ambushed the two policemen one night and threw them over a high bank into a river. The three

Indians were arrested, found guilty of murder and sentenced to be hanged, and they were hanged.
I was asked if I would look into the matter of the hanging, because it was alleged that they were all dropped through the trap door at the same time. The smallest of the Indians was in the middle; the two on the outside held him up and his neck was not broken. He strangled to death. Because of that being brought to my attention, and being asked if I would interest myself in it, I raised the matter in the British Columbia legislature. I was told by the attorney general of that day that I was not in a position to talk of capital punishment unless I had seen a man hanged.
I did not know then, and I do not know now, just what that had to do with it, but I was a very young man and that was the considered view of the attorney general, that I could not speak on capital punishment unless I had seen a man hanged. I went to see a man hanged, a 21 year old boy, the driver of a get-away car at a bank robbery where the teller was shot. Incidentally, the bank was only a block away from where I lived.
It was in the same year that I had my attention first drawn to capital punishment in the two ways I have told you, sir, that a friend of mine-and he was a very good friend of mine-in the hungry 1930's tried to maintain his farm and his family, and wandered all over British Columbia searching for employment. Well, there was no employment in British Columbia, and he went back to his home unannounced, sir. He walked in and found his best friend with his wife. He took up a shotgun and killed them both. He was accused of murder, found guilty and sentenced to hang. The sentence was commuted. May I just add, sir, that, he was paroled some three years ago and is a good citizen.
This is what created my interest in this question of capital punishment 25 years ago. And, sir, I do not think in all my time in public life I have made such an intense study of any subject as I have tried to make of this question of capital punishment, right or wrong.
Just like the mover of this bill, I have read everything, every study, every commission, every report I could put my hands on, anywhere in the world; and, Your Honour, I hope I can approach this from an unbiased position. I hope hon. members will accept what I say, based on a quarter of a century of study of this question; that I can stand in my place this afternoon in support of this bill and say that from analysis and study of the history of capital punishment in the world, I do not know of, I have never 79951-0-76
Capital Punishment
yet been able to find, one logical statement or position that can be taken in support of the retention of capital punishment. Emotionally, yes, you can talk for and against; but I say on the record and on the history I do not know of one factual, logical, reasonable, Christian basis for capital punishment.
For over 25 years I have received literally hundreds of letters from those who believe that we should maintain the death penalty, and their reasoning falls into these categories: (1) the bible is the authority and gives the right; (2) it is a deterrent to homicide; (3) it is a protection of the police forces; (4) because of the suffering of the loved ones and friends of the victim, the loved ones and the friends of the guilty person shall have to suffer, too.
These, sir, are the basic reasons I have been given as to why we should retain the death penalty. Under analysis, Mr. Speaker, these reasons will not stand up. Within the past three weeks in particular, sir, since the hon. member gave notice and filed his bill, I have received a number of letters, as a matter of fact most of them quoting the bible. I am not going into that now, but I say to those here who know the bible, and to some I can see who are not members of this house and who wear the cloth, that for every quotation that can be given from the bible saying "thou shalt kill" I will produce three that say "thou shalt not kill".
That is a fact. It is claimed that the retention of the death penalty is a deterrent to homicide. Records on penology throughout the world show that statement is not correct. We in Canada believe and maintain that we are a civilized people, but do we say that we are different from people in other parts of the world, in Belgium, Denmark, Holland, Luxembourg, Norway, Sweden, Portugal? Is there some difference between us? I do not think so. Do we take the position that the people of Canada are more criminally-minded than the peoples of the countries I have named? I do not think so. Then why should we maintain that as a deterrent to homicide in Canada we have to retain capital punishment, when it has been proved over a period of 100 to 150 years in other countries of the world that they have a lower homicide rate than we have, and they do not have the death penalty?
Read the record as placed before the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which considered this question for some three years. The last execution in Belgium was in 1863; the last execution in Denmark was in 1892; in Finland in 1826; in Holland in 1860, exactly 100 years ago; in Luxembourg in 1822; in Norway in 1876;

Capital Punishment
in Portugal in 1867, and in Rumania in 1838. To come closer to the present day, the last execution in Sweden was in 1919. For a period of 100 to 140 years there has been no death penalty in these countries, whose people are people of flesh and blood and emotions the same as the people of Canada.
What is the rate of homicide in these countries? Read the record; read the facts as given to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons by some of the world's most famous penologists. In most cases there is a lower homicide rate per
100,000	than we have in Canada. According to the last official figures I have the homicide rate for Canada was 1.2 per 100,000 of population. Let us take the countries that have had no death penalty for 100 years or more. In Holland, where the last execution took place 100 years ago, the homicide rate is 0.4 per 100,000; in Norway, 0.5; in Sweden, 0.8; in Switzerland, 1; in Denmark, 1, and in West Germany 1.2, the same as Canada. That is the record; those are the facts.
As was pointed out by the sponsor of the bill, if the death penalty is a deterrent then how do we explain the situation in the United States? I do not want to go into too much detail, because the hon. member dealt with this, but let us take the situation in the United States. Capital punishment was abolished in Michigan in 1847; in Wisconsin in 1853; in Maine in 1887; in Minnesota in 1911; in Rhode Island in 1952, and in North Dakota in 1895. In addition, a number of states that had capital punishment abolished it and then restored it. Tennessee abolished it in 1915 and restored it in 1919. Arizona abolished it in 1917 and restored it in 1919. Missouri abolished it in 1917 and restored it in 1919. Colorado abolished capital punishment in 1897 and restored it in 1901. I am not going through the list.
Let us look at the history of the states of the United States; those that have always had capital punishment, those that have abolished it as far back as 1847, as I have mentioned, and those that abolished it and restored it, and compare the ratio of homicide year by year. What is the story? As pointed out by the mover of the bill, the homicide rate has varied up and down in the same way as between abolitionist and non-abolitionist states. So the history of the countries of the world which are abolitionist and the history of the United States demonstrate that capital punishment is not a deterrent and has no bearing.
One phase of utmost importance to all of us is the protection of our police forces. If there were a sound argument that capital punishment is a protection for police forces,

that would be a very important factor in deciding whether we should retain or abolish capital punishment. I noted that the police representatives who appeared before the joint committee asked for retention for their protection. About two weeks ago I noticed in the press that the former commissioner of the R.C.M.P. was advocating the retention of capital punishment as a protection for our police forces.
But, sir, where is the evidence that it is a protection? May I repeat that if it is it should be retained, and that would be a powerful argument for its retention. But is it a protection? To the best of my knowledge only one study has ever been made anywhere in the world on the question of whether capital punishment is a protection for police forces. That study was made four or five years ago by Professor Sellin of the University of Pennsylvania, one of the world's outstanding penologists. He used his postgraduate class to conduct a study of this question. The chief of police of every town in the United States with a population of
10,000	or over was asked to send in a compilation of homicides in his city over a long period of years where policemen had been killed in the performance of their duties.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, to the best of my knowledge this is the only study that has ever been made of this question. When the replies were received they were tabulated at the university. What was found? It was found that there was no difference in the homicide ratio in the abolitionist states as compared with the non-abolitionist states. It was found that as the homicide ratio moved up and down year by year in the general picture for all states, it moved the same way with regard to the deaths of policemen who had been performing their duties in guarding the rights and property of the people. Hence on that basis, on that study-and it is the only one that we can find-it is not a deterrent to homicide generally nor does it afford added protection for the police force of a country. I am trying desperately, Mr. Speaker, to stand or to base my arguments on my reading of the facts and what has been discovered by the penologists of the world.
May I then move on just briefly to another plane and deal with something which was also mentioned by the mover of the bill and which had not come to my attention until this year. I have noted, as has he also, that of recent weeks in particular objections to the abolition of capital punishment from some people come forward on the basis that it is going to cost the taxpayers money. I know that in the past month I have received

a number of letters from people whose chief reason for maintaining capital punishment is that it will cost the taxpayers money to put prisoners in jail and keep them there for life instead of breaking their necks at the end of a rope.
I want to add my words to those of the mover and say that we have come to a "pretty pass" in Canada if our approach to penology or to murder is going to be on the basis of whether or not it costs the taxpayers money. If that is a valid argument-I say "if that is a valid argument"; in my opinion it is not-then there is only one thing to do and that is to go back to the law of 50 or 100 years ago when hanging was the penalty for almost every crime. Then you would save money.
Surely that is not an intelligent approach to this kind of question. May I just add that if it is, then perhaps in order to stamp out crime we ought to do what was done a few centuries ago when Wales was a monarchy. I forget the name of the king, but a few hundred years ago there was a king in Wales who determined that he was going to stamp out crime; and he stamped out crime in three years. He hanged 5,000 men, women and children in three years. That may have been the approach then but surely it is not our approach today.
I started off by telling the house how I became interested in this subject 25 years ago. I tried to give the house some of the facts that have been made available by the penologists of the world. I have tried very briefly to point out the ratio of homicides in various countries of the world and states of the United States, as between the abolitionist principle and the non-abolitionist principle. More than that, I do not think it is possible to do.
May I conclude in the way I began. If the bible means anything, it means Christianity. If it can be used by some as the foundation for society's right to put a man to death, then may I point out that the bible also has plenty to say about the sanctity of life and "Thou shalt not kill". World's records show that capital punishment is not a detriment to homicide, so why maintain it unless it is from a feeling of revenge and retribution? If, as the record shows, it is not an added protection to our police forces, then why should it be used as an argument for maintaining the death penalty? If in a situation the friends and the loved ones of the victim suffer, is that any reason why we should then say, "We demand that the loved ones and the friends of the murderer, who are innocent, shall also be made to suffer"? No matter how you look at the matter-emotionally, 79951-0-76*
Capital Punishment
as a Christian, statistically or factually-I feel firmly convinced that any thinking man or thinking woman or any parliament can come to only one conclusion, namely that capital punishment is inhuman, out of date and should be abolished.

Mr. Speaker, I find myself in a rather difficult position this afternoon following two such learned members who have given such great study to this matter. I am not going to put myself forward as an expert on their level. But notwithstanding that consideration, I must say at once that I completely reject the arguments they have put forward. I do not believe that in any way the principle of abolition of capital punishment reflects public opinion in this country. Indeed, it is rather surprising to me that people so far from public opinion could find themselves in the House of Commons.
I believe the situation is somewhat difficult, though, for us as members of parliament in connection with this matter. In rejecting the argument for the abolition of capital punishment I do not in any way indicate that I am satisfied with the present situation. I believe public opinion does demand that a change be made in the Criminal Code. But as to what extent that should go, I believe that matter could be much better debated on some of the other bills that will be coming before the house. While I do not want to go beyond the rules of debate here, I simply want to mention the fact that the hon. member for Burn-aby-Riehmond (Mr. Drysdale) has on the order paper a bill which I believe comes a great deal closer to meeting the wishes of the people of Canada in this regard than does the one now before the house.
I believe there are certain instances in which capital punishment or the death penalty does not act as a deterrent; and in those instances it is evident that the public want us to do something about removing the death penalty. In crimes of passion, I think it is quite clear that the death penalty does not act as a deterrent. But in general, having regard to the protection of our police officers, surely common sense would tell us that, if a man has committed a crime where he is going to be committed to life imprisonment, is being apprehended by a police officer and is armed, there is going to be the temptation for him, knowing that he can escape, knowing that if he shoots the police officer he can be no worse off than he was before. Surely it is going to act as a deterrent to that man if he knows that he is gding to be hanged, something which is considerably more abhorrent to him than is life imprisonment in most cases.

Capital Punishment
As I see it, it is the same in principle as the national defence of the country which is based on deterrence. Surely if it works on that principle-and it has worked successfully for many years now since the formation of NATO; we have had the principle of deterrence in our national defence; we have contained the enemy in that regard and it has been proven to have worked-then I suggest that in the case of criminals it will work to the same extent.
I do not feel that it would be proper for me at this time to go into exactly what length we should go in changing the law. I have mentioned the bill that I believe will meet the wishes of the people, and it will be coming forward for debate. As I see it at the present time, it will be useless for us to deal with all of the other bills in detail. I felt very much that I should like to have the opportunity of voting not only on this measure which gives us two choices. We can vote for abolition or we can vote for retention.
I feel that neither of those is what the public wants. They require a change in the Criminal Code. However, it would appear that the only course that we are now able to follow is to see that this bill is disposed of, that it be voted down, because I am absolutely certain that it will be, and I am also absolutely certain that that will be in accordance with the wishes of the public.
I say that as soon as possible we should direct ourselves toward changing the Criminal Code, perhaps in these respects. I believe that one of the things the public do not like about our present system is the hanging, and perhaps some other method of carrying out the death penalty should be instituted, such as the gas chamber or the electric chair. That is one way in which it might be changed. Second, certain crimes should be exempted, and perhaps we should consider the degree of evidence which should be required where there is the slightest doubt. Naturally, we would not want to see someone put to death in that event, and I think that is one other field where the public is concerned if a man is convicted on circumstantial evidence. It is a matter which needs a great deal of study.
As far as this bill is concerned, I believe the principle of abolition is absolutely wrong. It does act as a deterrent and we should retain the death penalty, but in a different form from that existing at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, as I enter this debate I wish to make it clear that I am for the abolition of the death penalty. However, in order to enable as many hon. members as possible to participate in this debate, my remarks will not be too long.

To hang or not to hang is the question of the hour. One can hardly pick up a newspaper or a magazine, or join a group in conversation, without finding opinions for and against capital punishment. This question has been treated on non-party lines and above politics, as indeed any measure of humanitarian interest should be, and without any partisan bickering. It is regrettable that questions of great importance to the welfare of the nation are not more often treated on similar non-party lines, because I think the country would be the better for it.
I would say that not very often does a subject of debate go deeply into the feelings of a large number of our constituents. It is undoubtedly because of such a widespread interest that a vote on non-party lines will be made on this bill. In voting for or against it we are expected to reflect the opinions of the majority of the Canadian people.
The issue appears to be as between two schools of thought; one thirsting after justice in a mood of vengeance, the other urging the practice of Christian charity and the rehabilitation of criminals. On the other hand, notable figures in the religious life of our country have gone on record as being in favour of abolition.
During the past several months we have been literally bombarded with letters and briefs. I have received, indeed, several within the last hour. I have one here consisting of several pages closely typewritten which I have not read, but I take it from the heading that the author is against abolition. Then there have been letters to editors of every newspaper in the country, many of which are replete with quotations from the old and new testaments, giving various interpretations to the scriptures, according to the view of the individual concerned. I am not going to quote the bible, Mr. Speaker, for the simple reason that I do not feel competent to interpret the writings in the old book; I prefer to leave that to spiritual advisers whose training and vocation qualify them to speak with authority on the subject of religion.
Some hold to the belief that fear of the death sentence is a restraining force -against murder. Personally, I share the views of those who believe that there is no valid guarantee that the fear of punishment by death is a definite deterrent. Consider the proportion of murders committed in circumstances of sudden passion which are not deterred by threat of the consequences. Crimes such as robberies, from which murder might result, are deliberately planned to avoid detection. Consider also the risk of executing an innocent person.

To those who would anticipate a rise in crimes leading to murder in the event of parliament approving this bill, I would point out that the experience of countries where capital punishment has long been abolished is, indeed, ample proof that such a conclusion is unfounded.
Here I wish to mention some of the countries which have had no death penalty for years. Luxemburg has had no dealth penalty since 1822, Belgium since 1863, Portugal since 1867, Holland since 1870, and Italy since 1890. It was restored in that country during the fascist regime, but it was again abolished in 1948. Norway has had no death penalty since 1905, Sweden since 1921, Denmark since 1930, Switzerland since 1942, and it is so in dozens of other nations, including several states of the union.
I would like now to quote from a report of a British select committee on the subject made in 1930, as follows:
Our prolonged examination of the situation in foreign countries has increasingly confirmed us in the assurance that capital punishment may be abolished in this country without endangering life or property or impairing the security of society.
If the remission of death sentences during the last two years by our government-and there were 31 out of a total of 38-is the criterion, then I would say that it has gone a long way to abolish the death penalty. So why not do it by an act of parliament, which is the voice of the people and not just the voice of the cabinet? There may be some justification to retain the death sentence for specific 'Crimes in time of war or for treason. I do not know the considerations which made the cabinet commute the death sentence of 75 per cent of those condemned to death by judges during the past two and a half years. No doubt there were good and sufficient reasons for those commutations, but in my humble opinion I believe that justice would have been best served if capital punishment was not mandatory in respect to murder.
In order to avoid the danger of a murderer sentenced to life imprisonment regaining his liberty after only 20 odd years, provided there has been good behaviour on his part, the Criminal Code should be amended to make the penalty 99 years. Assuming, then, that a person being so sentenced was 20 or 30 years old-the average age of a criminal- and that remissions for good behaviour would amount to 20, 25 or 30 years, if he lived to a ripe old age and had his sentence reduced by that extent he would still be close to 100 years old upon his release, and no one would begrudge the respite of a year or two which would probably be worse for him. This, I believe, would be a real deterrent and one
Capital Punishment
which would literally mean life imprisonment for certain crimes, a punishment which would be worse than death.
I have come to the conclusion, not without having made a deep study of this subject, having regard to the suffering caused to innocent people by criminals who commit murder that the time has come to do away with the archaic method of killing the guilty by hanging them by the neck until they are dead.

I should like at the beginning of my remarks to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) for having been instrumental in bringing before us today this bill which I wholeheartedly support. I want to commend him, too, on the excellence and the clarity of his presentation.
I should like, if I may to take the opportunity to express my admiration for some earlier pioneer efforts in the field which we are discussing today, earlier bills brought before this house by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who, I thought, spoke very effectively this afternoon and, before him-some considerable time before I came into this house-by Mr. Ross Thatcher.
I want to say a word also about the policy of the present government in respect to capital cases which come before it for consideration. The death penalty is still the law of Canada and over the last three years I have been more than gratified to observe that this penalty has been reserved for those cases which one could characterize as being most gruesome, the most clear-cut, the most premeditated type of killing. That, to my mind, is the kind of reservation which should always be applied so long as this law remains on the books of our country.
Once in a while from different quarters one hears some criticism of the frequency of the commutations. What the critics fail to appreciate is that the same Criminal Code which places upon the trial judge the mandatory obligation to impose the penalty of death upon a convicted murderer also confers upon the governor in council the right to review each sentence with a view to commuting it to a period of not less than two years imprisonment, thereby placing upon the government of the day the very important obligation of reviewing all such cases for the purpose of determining whether the awful penalty of the law should or should not be carried out.
There is, therefore, absolutely nothing inconsistent about a policy which requires a trial judge on the one hand mandatorially to impose the sentence of death, and upon a

Capital Punishment
The death penalty is not the answer to the problem of crime and of criminals. Crime has its cause and crime has its cure. Its causes are clear. They can be stated like the litany: they are slums, they are broken homes; they are poverty; they are drunkenness, divorce, lack of opportunity, lack of education. These are the causes of crime. As a lawyer, day after day, I see far too often, and still see far too often, in far too many cases those factors, or some of those factors, or a combination of all those factors. Those factors are the cause of crime; they are the common denominator in a great majority of cases that come before our courts from coast to coast day after day.
Why do you worry about your children? Why do you care what happens to your little boy? Why do you wonder where he has gone, how long he is going to be out, who he has been with? What do you fear, if not that by virtue of companionship^ with others or other places he will lead himself to the road of moral and social disaster? You check the background of every man who has been executed in Canada in the last 25 years and I wager you will find there are a good many cases in which there was no parent who displayed that kind of anxiety for him. Those are the things that we have to keep in mind.
Anatole France once said that the law had a majestic equality. He said, "The law equally forbids the rich and the poor from doing the following things: from sleeping under bridges; from begging alms on the streets and from stealing a loaf of bread". That may be the only thing he ever said that I will ever agree with, but it is a statement that causes one to sit back and to think. As legislators we should ponder less about the need for the penalty of death, and we should ponder more about co-operating with government to eradicate some of the roots from which crime stems; help clear up the slums in co-operation with provinces or municipalities; help build recreational centres to which underprivileged boys and girls can come to find opportunity that they are denied at home, to find friendship and affection that they are denied at home. Those are the sorts of things we should all be doing. We should be placing emphasis on prisons; we should be encouraging a continuance of the development of the present policy to modernize and humanize those places, places in which the emphasis will be upon the reformation and the reclamation of the people who live within them, places from which the graduates will leave restored to dignity and prepared to take their place in society.

The death penalty is out of date; it is not an answer, nor will it ever be. The slow march of civilization has brought us to a point in our history where we should be ready here and now to vote in favour of its abolition.
